definition: The vocabulary of machine instructions a processor understands, such as x86 or Arm. Software compiled for one ISA does not run natively on another, which is why ISA choice locks in ecosystems.
The instruction set used by Intel and AMD processors since the 1970s-80s. Only Intel and AMD hold the licences to build x86 server CPUs, and most legacy enterprise software is compiled for it.
A family of instruction sets licensed by Arm Holdings to chip designers, who pay licence fees and per-chip royalties. Grace, Vera, Graviton, Axion and Cobalt are Arm CPUs.
An open, royalty-free instruction set that anyone can implement. Start-ups such as Ventana, Rivos, Tenstorrent and Akeana design high-performance RISC-V cores as an alternative to Arm.
Arm's family of datacenter CPU core designs (N-series for efficiency, V-series for performance). Grace and Graviton4 both use Neoverse V2 cores.
A pre-integrated, pre-verified Arm block of cores, on-chip mesh and I/O that a licensee drops into its chip to save design time. It carries a higher royalty than licensing cores alone.

A per-chip payment to the owner of licensed technology, usually a percentage of the chip's selling price or a fixed fee per unit, on top of an upfront licence fee. Arm earns most of its revenue this way.

An Arm licence that lets a company design its own cores implementing the Arm instruction set, rather than using Arm's core designs. Apple, Qualcomm and NVIDIA (for Vera's Olympus cores) use this route.
NVIDIA's chip-to-chip link joining a Grace or Vera CPU to its GPUs at 900 GB/s (Grace) or 1.8 TB/s (Vera), several times a PCIe slot, with cache coherence so the GPU can use CPU memory directly.
Hardware that keeps every processor's cached copy of shared memory consistent, so a CPU and GPU can read and write the same data with ordinary pointers instead of explicit copies.
NVIDIA's name for a CPU and one or two GPUs joined by NVLink-C2C on one module, such as GH200 (one Grace, one Hopper) or GB200 (one Grace, two Blackwell).
Low-power DRAM originally made for phones, used by Grace and Vera instead of standard server DIMMs because it delivers more bandwidth per watt; it is soldered or mounted close to the CPU.
A compact, replaceable memory module carrying LPDDR5X chips, used with Vera so that low-power memory can be serviced like a normal DIMM.
Multiplexed-rank DIMM: a server memory module that interleaves two ranks to roughly double the data rate per channel (e.g. 8,800 MT/s), raising CPU memory bandwidth without more channels.
Converting a program's machine code from one instruction set (or form) to another while it runs. NVIDIA's Denver cores used a related 'dynamic code optimisation' scheme.
The general-purpose processor in an accelerated server that boots the system, runs the operating system, schedules work and moves data to and from the GPUs.
